units: the frame that carries the roof may be of wood or of metal
this frame passes the weight of the roof down to the load-bearing walls
thin strips of wood are nailed across it to take the covering
the covering described is a dark rock split into flat sheets
this covering lets the space under the roof breathe
a channel set at the bottom of the slope gathers the rainwater
that water is then sent into a vertical pipe
an opening cut into the slope brings light and air to the floor under the roof
this opening weakens the watertightness if it is poorly fitted
a specialist tradesman inspects the whole of it before the rainy season
text: A roof is an assembly of parts, and each one does a job of its own. The frame comes first, a skeleton of timber or of steel that holds the whole thing up and passes its weight down into the load-bearing walls. Thin strips of wood are then nailed across it, and the covering hangs from them. Slate, a dark rock that splits into flat regular sheets, keeps the rain out while letting the space underneath breathe. Along the bottom edge of the slope, a channel catches the water running off and feeds it into a vertical pipe, so that the walls below stay dry. Higher up, a dormer cuts through the slope to bring light and air to the top floor, and its surround has to be fitted with care, since any opening breaks the run of the covering. A roofer who knows the trade goes over every one of these parts before the wet season.

units: workmen were taking up a damaged floor at the top of an empty house
a workman's tool struck something hard under a board
an old piece of timber covered with notches came to light
the man in charge of the site halted the work
a restoration specialist came to look at the find the next day
she identified marks cut by the original builder
those marks showed in what order the structure was to be put together
the owner gave up the idea of replacing the structure
he chose to have it strengthened instead
the timber is left in view and protected by a pale coating
text: The work began at the top of a town house that had stood empty for two winters, where a rotten floor was being taken up board by board. Lifting the third plank, the workman felt his bar strike something hard underneath. He brushed the dust aside and freed an old blackened beam whose hidden face carried a row of even notches. The foreman stopped everything. A restorer of old buildings arrived the next morning, ran her palm along the grain, and knew the marks for what they were, cut by the carpenter who first raised the frame. Each sign, she explained, gave the order in which the pieces were meant to go together, the way words are numbered in a sentence taken apart. Told of it at the end of the week, the owner gave up replacing the frame and asked instead that it be strengthened. The beam still shows overhead, under a pale wax.

units: the water content of the wall must be checked before a lightweight partition goes up
a damp backing stops the finish from holding
the coating comes away in flakes at the first heating if the backing is wet
the line of the partition is marked with a taut string
a floor track out of level throws every upright off and makes the finish ripple
the bonding compound is mixed in small amounts because it sets quickly
a screw driven too deep damages the surface and weakens the board
laying the joint tape on a wet backing makes it swell and then crack
a gap left at the foot of the partition protects it from water rising from below
text: Check how much water the wall still holds before you put up a lightweight partition. Plaster will not grip a damp backing, and the skim coat lifts away in flakes the first time the heating goes on. Snap a taut line to mark where the wall will run, then fix the floor track. Get that track out of level and every upright inherits the fault, so the finished face ends up rippling. Mix the bonding compound in small amounts, since it stiffens fast and whatever is left over hardens in the bucket. Drive the screws home without punching through the paper, because a torn face costs the board much of its strength. Let the joints dry before you tape them. Tape laid over damp work swells and cracks later on. Leave a small gap at the foot of the partition as well, or any water rising from below will stain it.

units: neighbours in a low-lying district were suffering flooded cellars after heavy rain
the trouble had lasted since the end of summer
a study was commissioned by the local authority
the drainage network had been designed for ground that soaked up water
the yards paved over in concrete have done away with that absorption
the water reached the doorways of the houses and ran in under the doors
the paths will be covered with a loose stony material that lets water through
channels running along the walls will carry the water to a basin dug further off
the money comes from a grant and from a share paid by the owners
a first stretch will be finished before the rainy season
text: Since the end of summer, people living in a low-lying district have reported cellars filling up after every heavy downpour. A study ordered by the local authority found that the drainage network, laid out when the ground still soaked up rain, can no longer cope now that the yards have been paved over in concrete. Nothing sinks in any more. The water slides toward the doorsteps and works its way under the doors. The technical department has settled on an answer in two parts. The paths will be dug up and laid again with loose gravel, which lets the rain filter down instead of throwing it back at the buildings. Shallow channels will then run along the exposed walls and carry the flow to a holding basin cut into the ground well away from the houses. The money comes from a grant to the authority and a share paid by the owners. A first stretch is due before the rains.

units: two dwellings face each other across a narrow street
they have no feature in common
the house on the left has a pale wall finish
its openings are closed by painted wooden panels
above each opening on the left runs a visible oak beam
the house on the right has stone walls left bare
its openings are narrower and capped by a beam of hard rock
it is shielded by metal slats that slide instead of swinging
the first gives an impression of welcome, the second an impression of closure
the entrance steps differ too, one of wood hollowed by use, the other a massive slab
text: Two houses stand across a narrow street from each other, and they have nothing in common. The one on the left shows a wall finished in pale lime, cut by tall windows with painted wooden shutters. Above each opening runs an oak beam left in view, barely curved, which softens the flat face of the wall. The house opposite answers with bare stone, deeply raked at the joints, where the openings are narrower and capped by a thick lintel of hard rock. No shutter swings there. Metal slats slide down into a groove instead. The first looks welcoming and a little worn by wind and rain, the second looks shut, heavy, cut to stand up to weather. Even the steps at the two doors are unalike, wood hollowed by generations of feet on one side, a thick cold slab on the other.

units: the writer holds that buildings are pulled down too easily instead of being put back in order
his first complaint bears on the waste of materials still fit for use
careful dismantling costs more than quick demolition
his second complaint concerns the loss of the craftsman's hand skills
those skills die out together with the places that taught them
his third complaint takes aim at the disappointing comfort of new buildings
new work suffers from heat in the warm season and draughts in the cold one
the bill falls on whoever lives in the dwelling
his fourth complaint is that the occupants' attachment counts for nothing
he does not ask that everything be kept but demands proof that repair was impossible
text: Let us be blunt: we knock buildings down too fast and mend them far too rarely. First complaint, the waste. Sound roof timbers, tiles that could go straight back up, a solid oak stair, all of it goes into the skip because taking things apart with care costs more than one swing of a machine. Second complaint, the hand trades are dying out. Who can still point up a wall in lime, straighten a sagging lintel, split a slate without shattering it? Those skills fade along with the workshops that passed them on. Third complaint, the comfort we were promised never turns up. The new building bakes in summer, whistles in winter, and whoever lives there pays the bill. Fourth complaint, what the place meant to the people who lived in it counts for nothing in the decision. I am not asking that everything be kept. Just prove that no serious repair was possible.

units: the woman in question was raised near a site where rock is quarried
her father worked there as a quarryman
she watched blocks being cut before she cut them herself
she entered training in a workshop that puts old buildings back in order
her first notable commission was the replacement of a worn entrance step
she went on to harder work such as a split beam and a vault to be reset
she founded her own workshop about ten years after she began
she employs two workmen
she now teaches beginners, several of whom had no manual experience
she holds that this material calls for patience
text: The stonecutter grew up beside a limestone quarry where her father worked the face, and she watched blocks being split long before she held a chisel herself. She took up an apprenticeship in a restoration workshop as a girl, learned to read the grain of the rock, then landed her first real commission, cutting a new threshold for an old coaching inn whose step had worn through. Heavier jobs followed, a cracked lintel to make good, a vault to be reset stone by stone. Ten winters or so after she started, she opened a workshop of her own, and two hands work there beside her. Lately she gives part of her week to apprentices from every sort of background, several of whom had never picked up a tool. Stone, she says, forgives impatience badly, and what she mostly teaches is how to slow the hand down.

units: the visitor comes out of this renovated building with a feeling of oppression
that feeling comes from technical choices rather than from a quarrel over taste
an insulating skin was added in front of the old walls
this addition pushed the windows back into a deep recess
the view towards the outside is now obstructed
a stretched ceiling hides the timber structure that used to be in view
this concealment costs the place its perceived scale
the gravel floor was replaced by a smooth surface
that surface throws the sound back and makes the noise hard to bear
the critic approves of keeping the entrance step worn hollow by passing feet
text: You come out of this renovated hall feeling hemmed in, and the cause lies in what was built rather than in any quarrel over taste. The designers lined the old walls with an unbroken insulating skin, so the windows now sit at the far end of a deep trench and the eye stops short of the outside. The roof frame, once readable from one end of the building to the other, has vanished behind a stretched ceiling, and with it goes the scale that made the room feel generous. The floor of packed gravel gave way to a smooth screed, which throws voices back off the bare walls and turns a murmur into a din. One decision consoles. The old threshold was kept, worn hollow by generations of feet, a reminder that the place was in use before anyone set out to improve it.

units: the writer addresses his neighbour in writing
he raises the water channel fitted along the shared wall
that channel has been overflowing since the recent rain
the water is damaging the wall finish and laying the mortar bare
an inspection revealed a blockage made of leaves and an empty nest
a fixing bracket has given way and tipped part of the channel over
the writer offers to clean the channel himself before long
he offers to change the broken brackets and correct the fall
he suggests fitting a guard so that the trouble does not return
he asks his neighbour to agree to these proposals
text: Dear neighbor, I am writing about the gutter that runs along the wall our two houses share. Since the downpours of last week it has been spilling over halfway down its length, and the water is eating into the stucco, which is now pitted and showing the mortar underneath. I put a ladder up and had a look. The channel is packed with matted leaves and an abandoned nest, and one of the brackets has given way, which has tipped that section backward. Let me suggest three things. First, a thorough cleaning, which I can do myself before the week is out. Second, new brackets in place of the two that broke, at very little cost, with the fall toward the downpipe corrected a little. Third, a guard fitted over the mouth of the channel so that none of this happens again. Tell me whether that suits you.

units: the text compares building with a timber frame and building in concrete
the comparison arises when a client looks at two bids
timber allows quick assembly because the parts are prepared in a shop
its lightness allows shallower foundations
timber fears water and calls for wide roof overhangs
the points where timber meets the ground call for particular watchfulness
concrete stores heat and softens swings in temperature
it also cuts down noise from outside
making it carries a heavy environmental cost and its curing lengthens the work
the common answer joins a concrete base and a timber frame
text: Should you build with a timber frame or in concrete? The question comes up as soon as a client sets two bids side by side. What does timber offer? Quick assembly, parts cut and made ready in a shop, and a light structure that lets the foundations stay shallow. What is held against it? Its dislike of water, which calls for generous roof overhangs and steady attention wherever the wood meets the ground. What does concrete offer? Mass, which soaks up heat, evens out swings in temperature, and deadens the noise coming off the street. What is held against concrete? A heavy environmental cost in the making, and a schedule stretched by the time each pour needs to cure. So which one wins? The two are often combined, a solid base carrying a light frame, and that pairing serves the building better than a clean-cut choice.
